job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

passage: Carbon is a remarkable element because it forms strong covalent bonds by sharing electrons with other atoms, rather than transferring them. In these bonds, the shared electron pair is effectively owned by both participating atoms simultaneously, creating a stable connection. Carbon's unique ability to link with itself, known as catenation, is also seen in elements like silicon, though carbon does it most extensively. When we look at hydrocarbons, saturated compounds like alkanes contain only single bonds and are generally less reactive because they lack double or triple bonds that could easily break to accept new atoms. In contrast, unsaturated hydrocarbons can undergo addition reactions. Furthermore, substances in a homologous series share the same functional group and similar chemical properties, but their physical properties, such as melting points, change gradually as the molecular mass increases. Finally, when soap is used in hard water, the calcium and magnesium ions react with the soap to form an insoluble precipitate called scum, rather than the soap simply evaporating. This happens because the soap molecules cannot form effective micelles in the presence of these mineral ions.

items.evidence: In these bonds, the shared electron pair is effectively owned by both participating atoms simultaneously, creating a stable connection.
items.q: In methane's dot structure, who owns an electron pair shared between carbon and hydrogen?
options: Carbon and hydrogen together, at the same time
Only the atom that first brought the electrons
Only carbon, since it forms four bonds
Only hydrogen, since it gave its electron away
items.explain: A shared electron pair belongs to both bonded atoms at the same time.

wrong.why: thinks shared electrons belong to the atom that brought them
thinks carbon's four bonds make it own the electrons
confuses sharing with ionic transfer of electrons

items.evidence: Carbon's unique ability to link with itself, known as catenation, is also seen in elements like silicon, though carbon does it most extensively.
items.q: Which element besides carbon can also form chains by linking with itself?
options: Silicon, though less than carbon does
None, because only carbon can do this
Hydrogen, since it bonds well with carbon
Calcium, since it reacts with soap
items.explain: Catenation is also seen in silicon, but carbon does it most extensively.

wrong.why: thinks catenation is unique to carbon
picks an element that bonds with carbon, not itself
picks another element named in the passage

items.evidence: When we look at hydrocarbons, saturated compounds like alkanes contain only single bonds and are generally less reactive because they lack double or triple bonds that could easily break to accept new atoms.
items.q: Lots of hydrogen is mixed with an alkane like ethane. What will most likely happen?
options: It does not add, having only single bonds
It adds hydrogen once enough is supplied
It adds hydrogen fast, being full of energy
It adds hydrogen after its double bonds break
items.explain: Alkanes have only single bonds, with no double bonds to break and accept new atoms.

wrong.why: thinks enough reagent forces addition in alkanes
thinks saturated means full of energy and reactive
mixes up alkanes with unsaturated hydrocarbons

items.evidence: Finally, when soap is used in hard water, the calcium and magnesium ions react with the soap to form an insoluble precipitate called scum, rather than the soap simply evaporating.
items.q: Why does soap leave a white, sticky scum when used in hard water?
options: Minerals in the water react with the soap
The soap evaporates and leaves a residue
The soap's tail is pulled towards the water
The soap spreads into flat circles on top
items.explain: Calcium and magnesium ions in hard water react with soap to form insoluble scum.

wrong.why: thinks scum forms because soap evaporates
thinks the hydrophobic tail attracts water
thinks micelles are flat circles on the surface
